John Brady’s?

I am just thinking about to post this tune, but a little bit late.

Many tunes have several names, but this tune is called Custy’s, Karen Tweed’s, and John Brady’s at once! I guess this is originally John Brady’s composition, and Mary Custy learned it from Karen Tweed (the piano-accordeon player from Northamptonshire), and finally it was handed down to Michael MacGoldrick.

Here is the version in Am, played by Sharon Shannon and Tommy Peoples.

Origins of this tune

This tune was composed by John Brady, flute player, from Offaly, Ireland during the summer of 1983. It is called McIntyre’s Fancy after his wife’s niece because she liked the tune as it was being composed. It can be heard on the Beauties of Autumn, the LP by the Longridge ceili band, published by Comhaltas in 1983.

↳ Posted by feadog on April 25th, 2004.

McIntyre’s Fancy

This tune was written by John Brady, flute player from Offaly during the summer of 1983. It was originally written in Amin. and started with a high A2 instead of the usual Cnatural D. Siobhan O’Donnell learned it from Karen Tweed who learned if from Attracta Brady, John’s daughter, in the mid 80s.

Re: McIntyre’s Fancy

It’s interesting that Siobhan O‘Donnell says that she learned the tune from Karen Tweed, because in her book ’Drops Of Springwater‘ Karen Tweed says: “These two tunes were learned from Siobhan O’Donnell, a great flautist and singer from London. When I lived for a short time in Cricklewood, these tunes were part of a set of four jigs often played in sessions with her in a pub called ‘The Good Mixer’ in Camden Town.”
At any rate there can now be no doubt that the tune was written by John Brady and is called McIntyre’s Fancy. Whoever learned it from whom, Mary Custy learned it from Karen Tweed (it was her version of it that I heard first), and Michael McGoldrick learned it from Mary Custy (or her CD with Eoin O’Neill) and transposed it into the (pleasing) key of B minor.
It would be interesting to know what the other two jigs in the ‘Good Mixer’ set of 4 were…
Mary Custy and Eoin O’Neill play it with Cowboy’s Jig and a very nice version of The Stool of Repentance; and Michael McGoldrick plays it between Knocknamoe Jig and his own composition Trip To Brittany.
